newsitem.title: USA: Canada's Martin sees bright outlook for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin sees bright outlook for 1997.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin Sunday delivered an upbeat assessment about the outlook for the Canadian economy.

"The outlook for 1997 and beyond is bright,' he told the International Monetary Fund's policy-making Interim Committee. "Our progress toward deficit reduction and in keeping inflation low has translated into sharply lower interest rates."
The IMF has forecast that Canada's economic growth will pick up to 3.2 percent next year from 1.4 percent in 1996.
"Putting Canada's finances on a sound footing is the cornerstone of our approach," Martin said.
"Deficit reduction is not a priority only of the federal government," he added. "Seven of Canada's 10 provincial governments achieved balanced budgets or surpluses in the most recent fiscal year."

While some analysts have voiced concern that cutting budget deficits when growth is weak is counter-productive, Martin said many nations do not have the luxury of postponing those decisions because their finances are in such bad shape.

"Monetary policy in these countries should stand ready to offset any contractionary effects that might occur in the short-term from cuts in budget deficits," he added, in an apparent allusion to the situation in Europe.
Martin reiterated Canada's support for the sale of a modest amount of IMF gold to help finance stepped-up aid for debt-ridden poor nations.
"I would like to see the IMF Executive Board endorse the sale of five million ounces of gold sooner rather than later," he said.
Any sale, he added, should be carried out "in a gradual and transparent manner. This will ensure that the impact on world gold markets is negligible."
